items.stem: Which term is defined as the following: “Using frightening information or images in a health message to motivate behaviour change”?
items.answer: Fear arousal
items.markingKey: Fear arousal: using frightening information or images in a health message to motivate behaviour change. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Very frightening health messages can be less effective than mildly frightening ones. Reason (R): High fear can lead people to deny or avoid the message. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: Defensive avoidance explains the finding. [1]

items.stem: Describe Janis and Feshbach’s (1953) study.
items.answer: High-school students heard a lecture on dental hygiene with strong, moderate or minimal fear content (or no lecture). A week later, the minimal-fear group showed the greatest improvement in reported dental behaviour (36% net change) and the strong-fear group the least (8%).
items.markingKey: 1 mark procedure; 1 mark findings with data [2]

items.stem: After a dental health talk in Lima, students reported whether they had improved their tooth-brushing a week later. Strong fear: improved 6, did not improve 44; No talk: improved 4, did not improve 46. Identify which row has the highest proportion of “improved” students. Show how you worked this out.
items.answer: Strong fear (12.0%)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: percentages (or proportions) calculated for each row; 1 mark: correct row identified [2]

items.stem: Sipho recorded how many students in each fear condition improved their dental behaviour. Minimal fear: improved 24, did not improve 23; No talk: improved 5, did not improve 40; Moderate fear: improved 15, did not improve 34. (a) Calculate the percentage of students for Moderate fear that were “improved”. Give your answer to one decimal place. (b) Calculate the overall percentage of students in the table that were “improved”.
items.markingKey: (a) 15 ÷ (15 + 34) × 100 = 15 ÷ 49 × 100 = 30.6%. 1 mark working; 1 mark answer [2] (b) Total “improved” = 44; total = 141; 44 ÷ 141 × 100 = 31.2%. 1 mark totals; 1 mark answer [2]

items.stem: Ethan recorded how many students in each fear condition improved their dental behaviour. No talk: improved 3, did not improve 44; Strong fear: improved 9, did not improve 44; Moderate fear: improved 22, did not improve 28; Minimal fear: improved 20, did not improve 25. (a) Calculate the overall percentage of students in the table that were “improved”. (b) Identify which row has the highest proportion of “improved” students. Show how you worked this out.
items.answer: (a) 27.7% (b) Minimal fear (44.4%)
items.markingKey: (a) Total “improved” = 54; total = 195; 54 ÷ 195 × 100 = 27.7%. 1 mark totals; 1 mark answer [2] (b) 1 mark: percentages (or proportions) calculated for each row; 1 mark: correct row identified [2]

items.stem: “Janis and Feshbach’s (1953) study of fear arousal has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including self-report in your answer.
items.answer: Strength (controls): Students were randomly allocated to lectures that differed only in fear level, with a control group. Strength (usefulness): It warns health campaigners that strong fear may backfire. Weakness (generalisability): The sample was from one American high school in the 1950s, so attitudes may differ today and elsewhere. Weakness (self-report): Dental behaviour was self-reported, so students may have exaggerated improvements. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: A student writes: “The more frightening a health message is, the more people will change their behaviour.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Research (Janis and Feshbach) suggests moderate or low fear can be more effective; high fear can cause avoidance.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain the Yale model of persuasive communication.
items.answer: Persuasion depends on the source (credibility, attractiveness), the message (one- or two-sided, emotional or rational, fear level) and the audience (age, intelligence, initial attitude, self-esteem).
items.markingKey: 1 mark source; 1 mark message; 1 mark audience [3]

items.stem: Jonas compared tooth-care behaviours (out of 10) one week after a low-fear or a high-fear health message. Table: Recommended behaviours performed (out of 10) — Low fear: 7, 6, 5, 5, 4, 8. High fear: 3, 2, 5, 4, 6, 5. What is the range of scores for the low fear condition?

A health campaign in Lima showed 7 students a low-fear leaflet about tooth care and 7 students a high-fear leaflet with images of diseased gums. The number of recommended tooth-care behaviours (out of 10) performed a week later was recorded. Table: Recommended behaviours performed (out of 10) — Low fear: 6, 8, 9, 8, 8, 7, 8. High fear: 6, 6, 8, 7, 5, 5, 4. Using the mean scores, state one conclusion that can be drawn from these results.
items.answer: The low fear condition had a higher mean (7.7) than the high fear condition (5.9), suggesting that low-fear messages are more effective than high-fear messages.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: conclusion about the effect of the IV on the DV; 1 mark: supported with the means [2]

items.stem: Ines compared tooth-care behaviours (out of 10) one week after a low-fear or a high-fear health message. Table: Recommended behaviours performed (out of 10) — Low fear: 6, 6, 7, 8, 7, 0, 6. High fear: 2, 4, 4, 5, 7, 6, 4. (a) Write a null hypothesis for this study. (b) Describe one variable that should be controlled in this study and explain why.
items.answer: (a) There will be no difference in the number of recommended behaviours performed between students given a low-fear message and students given a high-fear message. (b) The same checklist and timing for all students.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: IV and DV both included (operationalised); 1 mark: correct form of hypothesis [2] (b) 1 mark: relevant control identified; 1 mark: explains how it would otherwise act as a confounding variable [2]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that health promotion is most effective when it targets whole communities?
items.answer: Arguments for: Farquhar et al. (1977) reduced cardiovascular risk factors through community media campaigns. Community approaches reach many people at once. Arguments against: School programmes (Tapper et al., Food Dudes) and worksite schemes (Fox et al., 1987) can be more targeted. Individual factors such as unrealistic optimism and self-efficacy limit change. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. items.stem: A health campaign in Santiago showed 8 students a low-fear leaflet about tooth care and 8 students a high-fear leaflet with images of diseased gums. The number of recommended tooth-care behaviours (out of 10) performed a week later was recorded. Table: Recommended behaviours performed (out of 10) — Low fear: 8, 5, 10, 9, 6, 8, 8, 8. High fear: 6, 5, 7, 8, 5, 5, 6, 1. (a) Write a directional (one-tailed) hypothesis for this study. (b) Explain one ethical issue that the researcher should consider in this study. (c) Suggest one improvement to this study and explain how it would improve the validity or reliability of the results. (d) Explain why a repeated measures design might have been used instead, and one problem this would cause.
items.answer: (a) Students given a low-fear message will perform more recommended behaviours than students given a high-fear message. (b) Frightening images could upset students, so they should be warned and debriefed. (c) Randomly allocate participants to the conditions, to reduce the effect of participant variables. (d) Repeated measures removes participant variables because the same people do both conditions, but order effects (practice or fatigue) and demand characteristics become more likely; counterbalancing would be needed.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: IV and DV both included (operationalised); 1 mark: correct form of hypothesis [2] (b) 1 mark: ethical guideline named; 1 mark: applied to this study [2] (c) 1 mark: improvement; 1 mark: how to do it; 1 mark: effect on validity/reliability explained [3] (d) 1 mark: advantage of the alternative design; 1 mark: problem it causes; 1 mark: applied to this study [3]

items.stem: Describe the findings of Fox et al. (1987).
items.answer: After a token economy was introduced at two open-pit mines, workers earned stamps for working without accidents or injuries; the number of days lost through injury and the costs of accidents fell sharply and remained low for years.
items.markingKey: 1 mark procedure; 1 mark findings [2]

items.stem: Describe Farquhar et al.’s (1977) three-community study.
items.answer: One town received a two-year mass media campaign on heart disease risk; a second received the media campaign plus face-to-face instruction for high-risk people; a third was a control. Risk factors fell in both campaign towns, especially with face-to-face instruction.
items.markingKey: 1 mark design; 1 mark findings [2]

items.stem: A primary school in Cairo wants children to eat more vegetables at lunch. Suggest how a Food Dudes-style programme could be used.
items.answer: Show videos of heroic peer characters who eat vegetables and reward children with small prizes for tasting and eating them.
items.markingKey: 1 mark modelling; 1 mark rewards [2]

items.stem: A primary school in Nairobi wants children to eat more vegetables at lunch. (a) Explain why this programme might work, using learning theory. (b) Explain one problem with the programme.
items.answer: (a) Children imitate admired models (social learning) and rewards reinforce eating vegetables (operant conditioning). (b) Eating may decrease when rewards stop, and changes at school may not transfer to home.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark problem; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: Evaluate Fox et al.’s (1987) token economy for mine safety, including a discussion of usefulness.
items.answer: Strength (ecological validity): It took place in real workplaces over several years with real accidents measured. Strength (usefulness): It reduced injuries and saved money, so other industries could adopt similar schemes. Weakness (controls): There was no control mine, so other changes over time might explain the improvement. Weakness (reporting): Workers might have hidden minor accidents to keep their tokens, so accidents may have been under-reported. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Identify the term for the following: “The belief that one is less likely than other people to experience negative events”.
items.answer: Unrealistic optimism

items.stem: Explain how unrealistic optimism can prevent people from changing unhealthy behaviour.
items.answer: If people believe they are less at risk than others (“it won’t happen to me”), they see health messages as relevant to other people and see no need to change.
items.markingKey: 1 mark belief; 1 mark consequence [2]

items.stem: Explain why self-efficacy is important in health behaviour change.
items.answer: People who believe they can succeed (for example in quitting smoking) are more likely to try, persist and recover from setbacks, so health promotion should build confidence as well as giving information.
items.markingKey: 1 mark belief in ability; 1 mark effect on persistence [2]

items.stem: Mei, aged 19, from Singapore, smokes and says: “Smoking is bad for some people, but I’m young and healthy so it won’t affect me. Anyway, I could never quit.” Identify two individual factors that may prevent Mei from changing behaviour.
items.answer: Unrealistic optimism (“it won’t affect me”) and low self-efficacy (“I could never quit”).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: “Weinstein’s (1980) study of unrealistic optimism has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including usefulness in your answer.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): It explains why general health warnings fail and suggests personalised risk information. Weakness (generalisability): Participants were American college students, who may be more optimistic than other groups. Weakness (self-report): Ratings were hypothetical and may not predict real health behaviour. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that fear arousal is an effective way of promoting health? In your answer, you may refer to Yale model and individual differences.
items.answer: Arguments for: Fear can attract attention and increase perceived severity. Some campaigns using fear appeals have changed behaviour (for example warnings about fire safety). items.answer: Unrealistic optimism (“it won’t affect me”) and low self-efficacy (“I could never quit”).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Ana compared tooth-care behaviours (out of 10) one week after a low-fear or a high-fear health message. Table: Recommended behaviours performed (out of 10) — Low fear: 7, 6, 6, 7, 8, 6, 7, 9. High fear: 5, 5, 3, 5, 4, 3, 4, 6. (a) Identify the independent variable (IV) and the dependent variable (DV) in this study. (b) The participants were people who responded to a poster in a library in Madrid asking for participants. Identify the sampling technique used and explain one weakness of it.
items.answer: (a) IV: the level of fear in the health message (low or high). DV: the number of the 10 recommended tooth-care behaviours performed one week later (self-report checklist). (b) Volunteer sampling. Weakness: only people who saw the poster and chose to respond took part, so the sample may be unrepresentative.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: IV; 1 mark: DV, operationalised [2] (b) 1 mark: sampling technique; 1 mark: weakness explained [2]

items.stem: Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of Weinstein’s (1980) study of unrealistic optimism. Include at least one point about sample.
items.answer: Strength (sample): A sizeable group of students rated many different events, so the pattern was consistent. Strength (usefulness): It explains why general health warnings fail and suggests personalised risk information. Weakness (self-report): Ratings were hypothetical and may not predict real health behaviour. Weakness (generalisability): Participants were American college students, who may be more optimistic than other groups. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: Which term is defined as the following: “How expert and trustworthy the person or organisation delivering a message is perceived to be”?
items.answer: Source credibility
items.markingKey: Source credibility: how expert and trustworthy the person or organisation delivering a message is perceived to be. [1]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) In a revision session, a student says: “An expert source is usually more persuasive than a non-expert.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Describe Janis and Feshbach’s (1953) study.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Credibility increases persuasion according to the Yale model. (b) High-school students heard a lecture on dental hygiene with strong, moderate or minimal fear content (or no lecture). A week later, the minimal-fear group showed the greatest improvement in reported dental behaviour (36% net change) and the strong-fear group the least (8%).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2] (b) 1 mark procedure; 1 mark findings with data [2]

items.markingKey: Ordered scores: 7, 7, 8, 9, 9, 9, 10; median = 9. 1 mark: data ordered; 1 mark: correct median [2]

items.stem: Design a field experiment to investigate whether a classroom programme using peer models increases children’s fruit and vegetable consumption. Your plan must include: how the dependent variable will be measured, the sampling technique and ethical issues.
items.answer: Method: a field experiment. Manipulate the IV in a natural everyday setting; participants may not know they are being studied; standardise as much of the procedure as possible. Variables: IV: programme or no programme; DV: portions of fruit and vegetables eaten at lunch. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Mumbai, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: Evaluate Janis and Feshbach’s (1953) study of fear arousal, including a discussion of controls.
items.answer: Strength (controls): Students were randomly allocated to lectures that differed only in fear level, with a control group. Strength (usefulness): It warns health campaigners that strong fear may backfire. Weakness (generalisability): The sample was from one American high school in the 1950s, so attitudes may differ today and elsewhere. Weakness (self-report): Dental behaviour was self-reported, so students may have exaggerated improvements. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: Identify the term for the following: “A programme in which people earn tokens for target behaviours that can be exchanged for rewards”.
items.answer: Token economy
items.markingKey: Token economy: a programme in which people earn tokens for target behaviours that can be exchanged for rewards. [1]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A student writes: “Health promotion in schools can only provide information.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Describe the findings of Fox et al. (1987).
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Programmes such as Food Dudes use modelling and rewards to change behaviour. (b) After a token economy was introduced at two open-pit mines, workers earned stamps for working without accidents or injuries; the number of days lost through injury and the costs of accidents fell sharply and remained low for years.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2] (b) 1 mark procedure; 1 mark findings [2]

items.stem: Explain one weakness of Fox et al.’s (1987) token economy for mine safety in terms of controls.
items.answer: There was no control mine, so other changes over time might explain the improvement.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to controls; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: A primary school in Accra wants children to eat more vegetables at lunch. (a) Explain why this programme might work, using learning theory. (b) Explain one problem with the programme.
items.answer: (a) Children imitate admired models (social learning) and rewards reinforce eating vegetables (operant conditioning). (b) Eating may decrease when rewards stop, and changes at school may not transfer to home.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark problem; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: ‘Health promotion is most effective when it targets whole communities.’ Discuss this view. In your answer, you may refer to effectiveness and generalisability.
items.answer: Arguments for: Farquhar et al. (1977) reduced cardiovascular risk factors through community media campaigns. Community approaches reach many people at once. Arguments against: School programmes (Tapper et al., Food Dudes) and worksite schemes (Fox et al., 1987) can be more targeted. Individual factors such as unrealistic optimism and self-efficacy limit change. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.answer: A person’s belief in their ability to carry out a behaviour successfully.

items.answer: (a) The low fear condition had a higher mean (6.7) than the high fear condition (4.1), suggesting that low-fear messages are more effective than high-fear messages. items.stem: Isla, aged 19, from Santiago, smokes and says: “Smoking is bad for some people, but I’m young and healthy so it won’t affect me. Anyway, I could never quit.” (a) Identify two individual factors that may prevent Isla from changing behaviour. (b) Suggest how a health promoter could address Isla’s unrealistic optimism. (c) Suggest how Isla’s self-efficacy could be increased.
items.answer: (a) Unrealistic optimism (“it won’t affect me”) and low self-efficacy (“I could never quit”). (b) Give personalised risk information (for example lung function testing) and examples of young people harmed by smoking. (c) Set small achievable goals, provide support and show similar people who have quit successfully.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark strategy; 1 mark explained [2] (c) 1 mark strategy; 1 mark explained [2]
